title: "A tiny cog in a large machine": Digital Taylorism in the translation industry
author: Joss Moorkens

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Translation work: Automation erodes autonomy unevenly
st.an: Moorkens strongly accepts the cluster’s shift from job counts to the organisation and control of surviving work, and materially develops it through the Digital Taylorism mechanism: fragmented tasks, rigid monitoring and platform dependence can reduce autonomy, meaning and skill development. He also strengthens the cluster’s balanced account by recognising efficiency, flexibility and trusted agency relationships while advocating sustainable work design and shared responsibility.
qs: In order to maximise efficiency and inspired by similar moves in the tech industry and predictions for Industry 4.0, large translation companies have begun to break tasks down into smaller chunks and to rigidly define and monitor translation processes.
The problem is that DT removes that autonomy, potentially leaving a repetitive role of relatively meaningless, rigidly defined and unsatisfactory tasks.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s work-redesign thesis through an adjacent knowledge-work domain. It shows that automation and task decomposition can undermine context, agency, mastery and accountability, and materially extends the cluster by advocating worker participation and control in iterative redesign. Its evidence concerns translation rather than legal AI, so it does not directly establish legal capability or verification claims.
qs: For example, he suggests that workers participate in a “cyclic and evolutionary procedure of continuous reﬂection and work redesign during which improvements are regularly explored, reﬂected upon, and evaluated” (Brödner 2009: 66).
However, mastery is difficult to achieve when carrying out varied decomposed and non-challenging tasks.

kp.k: Digital Taylorism combines task fragmentation with intensified surveillance
kp.d: Moorkens analyses translation and localisation rather than legal services. His central argument is that large providers increasingly decompose projects, prescribe methods and monitor workers to maximise efficiency. Digital Taylorism extends scientific management through technologies capable of quantifying and supervising knowledge work.
qs: large translation companies have begun to break tasks down into smaller chunks and to rigidly define and monitor translation processes.

This is the key difference between Taylorism and DT: jobs are standardised, methods documented, but now new technologies enable more varied and invasive monitoring and surveillance of workers to ensure that their role is carried out as expected

kp.k: Freelance dependence magnifies unequal power and worker replaceability
kp.d: The author argues that translation differs from technology-sector employment because most translators are freelancers. Outsourcing saves employment and office costs, while isolation and tightly restricted tasks weaken collective organisation and make workers interchangeable. Dependence on a single provider increases vulnerability to unilateral changes; nevertheless, some workers prefer small tasks within portfolio careers.
qs: The main difference is that most translators work on a freelance basis, and as such are likely to have less power and agency than direct employees
By working as a small and interchangeable part within a system of DT, they can be swapped out without any detrimental effect to the system as a whole.
On the other hand, not every worker wants to commit to a single employer or role, and they may prefer to work on small tasks as part of a portfolio career

kp.k: Historical efficiency gains did not guarantee shared prosperity
kp.d: Moorkens contrasts Taylor’s prediction that productivity would increase demand and benefit employers and employees with historical criticisms: documented, simplified tasks permitted lower-skilled labour, lower pay and potential automation. Walker and Guest’s 1952 interviews with 180 assembly-line workers found satisfaction with pay but alienation and weak commitment; the article reports correlations between mass-production processes, absenteeism and resignations.
qs: In practice, financial benefits did not necessarily accrue to both employers and workers.
the work could be carried out by less-skilled workers for less pay, and, potentially, automated.
These workers are generally satisfied with pay rates but are otherwise reportedly alienated and uncommitted.

kp.k: Cloud tools enable worker profiling and predictive management
kp.d: The article reports that cloud-based translation tools support real-time and logged monitoring. Garcia describes profiling by speed, quality and translation type; TAUS proposed an efficiency score based on words and edits per hour. Góis and Martins (2019) used keystroke data from 332 post-editors to predict future post-editing time. Moorkens also reports Ajunwa’s warning that automated hiring can amplify existing bias and that worker data may be sold.
qs: The tools used for translation and localisation processes are increasingly cloud-based, permitting monitoring of work in real time and in logs.
Góis and Martins (2019) attempt this, using keystroke data from 332 post-editors to predict future post-editing time.
Ajunwa (forthcoming) highlights the risk that this data may be sold and notes how automated hiring decisions based on such data is likely to amplify rather than remove existing bias.

kp.k: Consolidation and investor pressures encourage commodification
kp.d: Moorkens links consolidation, shareholder incentives and short-term returns to rate pressure and intensified work. Graham tracked 82 translation and interpreting acquisitions between 2016 and September of 2019. Kronenberg documented RWS acquisitions alongside unilateral payment changes and strong stock performance. These examples support the author’s critique, rather than establish an industry-wide causal estimate.
qs: Graham (2019) tracked 82 acquisitions of translation and interpreting companies between 2016 and September of 2019.
Kronenberg (2018) created a timeline of acquisitions by the company RWS, with notes of unilateral changes to payment conditions and rates imposed concurrently with strong stock market performance.
The imposition of new conditions and rates by RWS and Lionbridge (Llorens 2010) demonstrates the commodification of translation and a lack of care about motivation and satisfaction for translators.

kp.k: Complex production networks multiply narrowly specified roles
kp.d: The article describes role proliferation as projects are subdivided and cloud technologies integrated. Website checks on October 18th 2019 found 18 production-network roles at Lionbridge and 34 different roles at Transperfect, excluding accounts, management and marketing. Bond’s 2018 LinkedIn search identified over 600 job titles in language service providers. Moorkens argues that such networks offer specialised tasks but can weaken trust and diffuse responsibility.
qs: A LinkedIn search by Bond (2018a) identified over 600 different job titles in language service providers.
These roles offer translators opportunities to do highly-specified tasks within a translation production network.
when a single person cannot be identified or held responsible when a problem occurs

kp.k: Near-live delivery and agile updates fragment translation
kp.d: Reported production examples illustrate the speed-fragmentation mechanism. Netflix’s Chelsea workflow served over 190 countries less than 34 hours after taping, distributing slices to over 200 translators. Iyuno offered a two-hour turnaround for 45-minute Korean dramas, using 15-minute chunks, wikis and neural MT. Software-as-a-service and agile games development similarly generate incremental, decontextualised updates and pressure teams to expand or work additional shifts.
qs: the average size of translation tasks has fallen dramatically, even though overall volumes are rising

Iyuno Media (who received venture capital funding from Softbank Ventures in 2018 (Bond 2019)) offer an astonishing two-hour turnaround for translation of 45-minute premium Korean dramas into English, breaking content down into 15-minute chunks and translating with the aid of wikis and neural MT on their own proprietary cloud platform (Puttock 2018).
a constant update cycle has further decontextualized content for translation.

kp.k: Machine translation reallocates human work into piecemeal post-editing
kp.d: Unbabel provides the article’s concrete example of an MT-centred production system: automatic quality estimation routes selected sections to crowd post-editors, often for real-time customer support. Terminologists, translation analysts, linguistic annotators and NLP processing support the workflow. The article reports US$91m in external funding and notes the scaling and return pressures associated with venture capital.
qs: Unbabel’s platform uses MT for initial translation, followed by automatic quality estimation (QE).
Depending on QE results, sections of text are distributed to the crowd for MT post-editing on a piecemeal basis.
Unbabel are unusual in that they are very well resourced, having received US$91m in external funding

kp.k: Fragmentation limits ethical visibility and interpersonal trust
kp.d: Moorkens argues that workers who cannot see a project’s final purpose may be unable to exercise ethical judgement. He extends this concern from technology workers to MT researchers and translators handling decomposed projects. Fragmented workflows require translators to trust buyers, while monitoring signals distrust in the opposite direction; automated project management and short platform relationships further impede interpersonal trust.
qs: Workers who are unable to answer these questions risk contributing to projects to which they are ideologically opposed.

Again, the overall purpose of the project may be obscured within such a fragmented workflow, requiring trust on the part of the translator, whereas increased monitoring evinces a lack of trust on the part of the translation buyer or employer.
This is especially true for networks in which project management is automated (Sakamoto 2018) and in crowdsourcing scenarios.

kp.k: Platform efficiencies coexist with depersonalisation and dependency
kp.d: Pielmeier and O’Mara (2020) reported portal use by 89% of 6925 respondents; 69% said portals streamlined work and 56% said they depersonalised client relationships. Moorkens distinguishes these portals from riskier general crowd platforms, where work or profiles may be rejected without explanation or compensation. Cloud dependence also exposes workers to discontinuation, changed terms and regional access restrictions outside their control.
qs: Working via an online platform or portal has also become commonplace for many freelance translators, with 89% of 6925 respondents to Pielmeier and O’Mara (2020) saying that they use them.
69% of respondents said that these portals streamline their work, but 56% said that they depersonalise the client relationship.
workers on many platforms may have work rejected or their profile terminated without explanation or compensation.

kp.k: Restricted tasks undermine intrinsic motivation and professional development
kp.d: Using Herzberg’s motivation-hygiene model, Moorkens argues that fragmented work limits achievement, recognition, responsibility and growth while potentially worsening extrinsic sources of dissatisfaction. He distinguishes freelancers’ pre-existing lack of a career ladder from DT’s additional restriction of expertise and authority. Rodríguez-Castro’s 2016 research identified project completion, task variety and pride as crucial satisfaction factors.
qs: Removing segments of text from their context limits the abilities of translators to use their key linguistic and intratextual skills.

For freelance workers the lack of a defined career path is not a direct result of DT, but DT mitigates against gaining expertise or assuming authority by strictly limiting the scope of work and dictating how the work is to be done.
successful completion of projects, ability to perform a wide variety of tasks, and intrinsic pride in their work

kp.k: Irish survey reports isolation and large-agency concerns
kp.d: The article presents qualitative evidence from a 2016 Irish-English translator survey with 99 participants, including public servants, freelancers, self-employed translators and company owners; many did not complete every section. Seven of 57 responses about role changes mentioned additional workflow tasks, while 22 of 54 responses about industry threats cited large translation companies. Comparative analysis reported lower purpose and greater isolation among freelancers. Moorkens acknowledges that this was neither a major nor highly technologized language pair.
qs: The survey had 99 participants, although many did not complete all sections.
if working for large agencies, we are now just a tiny cog in a large machine
22 of 54 participants who responded to a question about the main threat to the industry wrote about the behaviour of ‘large translation companies’.
freelance translators appear to have a lower sense of purpose from their work and feel more isolated than directly employed company and public service translators.

kp.k: Flexibility benefits do not eliminate insecurity or lost meaning
kp.d: The author recognises that remote freelance work can support caring commitments, relocation and portfolio careers. In Pielmeier and O’Mara’s 2020 survey, 91% of 6003 freelancers liked flexible hours but only 43% reported a sense of purpose. Reported negatives included fluctuating income, irregular work, missing benefits and stress. Moorkens’s qualification is that flexibility is especially valuable when accompanied by autonomy, which DT can remove.
qs: 91% of 6003 freelancers said that they like the flexibility of hours offered by their profession, but only 43% said that it gave them a sense of purpose.
fluctuating income, irregular work, lack of benefits, and stress
The problem is that DT removes that autonomy, potentially leaving a repetitive role of relatively meaningless, rigidly defined and unsatisfactory tasks.

kp.k: Automation risks skill degradation and constrained career progression
kp.d: Moorkens cites Parasuraman and colleagues’ general warning that poorly designed automation can reduce system awareness, encourage excessive trust and degrade skills; this is not presented as a measured translation outcome. He also reports broader labour-market polarisation and recommendations to specialise at the high end of translation. Specialisation depends on ability and networks, and a hollowed-out middle may obstruct progression.
qs: poorly-designed automation could result in reduced system awareness, placing too much trust in the machine, and skill degradation
there will come a time when the human operator will not be as skilled in performing that function.
This is one obvious solution for some translators, although the hollowing out of the middle section of the market may make it more difficult to climb to the high end.

kp.k: Sustainable work balances efficiency with stakeholder development
kp.d: Drawing on sustainable-work-system scholarship, Moorkens recommends balancing short-term productivity and profitability with long-term learning, innovation and regeneration of human, social and natural resources. He connects this framework to UN Sustainable Development Goal 8, professional growth and future generations. Worker participation, control and recovery time are proposed safeguards, although freelancers’ uncertainty and involuntary unemployment can make refusing excessive work difficult.
qs: A sustainable work system does not prioritise one stakeholder over another.
The additional aspect in a sustainable work system is consideration of future generations, restricting activities that will delimit their agency or satisfaction of their needs.
increased work demands may cause less stress if a working person has control over the working process
Thus it becomes difficult for the freelancer to turn down work offered via the agency or platform

kp.k: Reform requires providers, workers, policymakers and educators
kp.d: Moorkens recommends diversifying clients, collective action where possible, stronger worker empowerment, sustainable provider relationships and support for translator organisations. He acknowledges competition on cost and speed, and legal or organisational barriers to collective action. Trainers should teach business ethics and contemporary practices, including decisions about data harvesting. His concluding recommendation includes environmental costs of automation and employer responsibility for motivation and satisfaction.
qs: At the very least, it makes sense for translators to diversify their agencies or clients so as to protect themselves from unilateral action or work practices that are demotivating and unsatisfactory.
Even with collective action, one stakeholder group will struggle to change the ecosystem.

There is also an onus on translator trainers to introduce business ethics and to highlight contemporary work practices in order to prepare students for future roles as both translators and translation industry workers.
This necessitates translation employers bearing some responsibility for the satisfaction and motivation of workers, as a sustainable industry will ultimately benefit all stakeholders.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Moorkens argues that machine translation, cloud platforms and digitally monitored task decomposition reorganise translation into tightly specified production workflows, with consequences for autonomy, trust, expertise and job satisfaction.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about translation, not legal services. Its argument concerns digital Taylorism broadly, rather than attributing every change to AI. Moorkens describes machine translation integrated with automatic quality estimation and selective human post-editing, alongside cloud-based surveillance and fragmented work allocation. These workflows create specialised roles and enable rapid delivery, but can make freelancers more interchangeable, obscure a project's purpose, dilute responsibility and restrict opportunities to develop expertise. He argues that reduced autonomy and repetitive, decontextualised tasks threaten motivation and long-term sustainability. He also anticipates continued automation in the cost-sensitive lower end of the translation market and suggests that a hollowing-out of its middle could make advancement to high-end specialist work harder. These are differentiated claims about workflow change and labour conditions, not a quantified prediction of wholesale translator replacement.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence combines reported industry workflows, workforce and satisfaction surveys, website observations, and literature on work organisation and automation.
pts.d: Moorkens describes Unbabel's MT–quality-estimation–post-editing pipeline using cited 2019 presentations, and reports Iyuno's two-hour turnaround for translating 45-minute Korean dramas through chunking, wikis, neural MT and a proprietary cloud platform. His October 2019 website checks found 18 production-network roles at Lionbridge and 34 at Transperfect, with specified exclusions for the latter; these indicate workflow differentiation rather than measured AI job creation. He cites research using keystroke data from 332 post-editors to predict post-editing time, without reporting predictive performance. Survey evidence includes 6,925 respondents on portal use, 6,003 freelancers on professional satisfaction, and a 2016 Irish-English translator survey with 99 participants and varying question-level response counts. These findings support descriptions of experiences and associations, not an isolated causal estimate of AI's effect. The skill-degradation warning draws on Parasuraman and colleagues' general automation framework; the job-polarisation discussion draws on broader labour-market literature rather than a translation-specific displacement estimate.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article describes developments observable by 2019–2020 and gives conditional, undated warnings rather than a dated automation forecast.
pts.d: Published in 2020, the article draws substantially on contemporary industry examples and surveys, including the 2016 Irish-language survey and October 2019 company website observations. Its concerns are strongest in large-provider, crowd-mediated, agile-localisation and near-live multimedia workflows where speed and cost dominate. Risks depend on how work and automation are designed, the extent of worker autonomy, and the strength of relationships with buyers. Moorkens explicitly recognises that flexible, project-based work can suit portfolio careers, caring commitments and remote work, and that some agencies maintain long-term relationships rather than competing solely on cost. High-end specialisation is presented as an option for translators with the necessary ability and network, not a universal solution. Recommendations for balancing efficiency with sustainable work are normative proposals, not demonstrated or time-bound outcomes.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The main affected groups are freelance and crowd translators, large language service providers, specialist translators, translation buyers and translator trainers.
pts.d: Freelancers, particularly those dependent on one provider, face reduced bargaining power and exposure to unilateral changes in conditions. Crowdworkers face interchangeability, reputational monitoring and possible rejection or termination without compensation. Subtitlers and software or games localisers encounter fragmented material and accelerated update cycles. Large providers gain monitoring, allocation and data-gathering capabilities, while complex production networks create checking, terminology, annotation and coordination roles. Clients and audiences receive faster multilingual delivery, but diminished context and fragmented responsibility may affect trust and accountability. High-end specialists may retain strong prices and satisfaction where their expertise and networks permit. Moorkens assigns employers responsibility for worker motivation and asks trainers to prepare future translators and industry decision-makers to address ethics, work practices and data harvesting.
